name: Zorn v. Linton
court: Supreme Court of the United States
topic: Qualified immunity, clearly established prong; rear wristlock pain compliance on a passively resisting protester after verbal warnings
summary: A Vermont sergeant removing sit in protesters from the state capitol used a rear wristlock to lift a woman who refused repeated requests to stand, after warning her that he would use more pain compliance. The Second Circuit denied qualified immunity, relying on its earlier Amnesty America decision. The Supreme Court summarily reversed, holding that the Second Circuit failed to identify a case where an officer using a routine wristlock on a protester after a verbal warning, without more, was held to have violated the Constitution, and that a general principle against gratuitous pain compliance lacks the specificity needed to clearly establish the law. Three Justices dissented. It is taught as the current statement of how specific the law must be to defeat qualified immunity in a control hold case.
coverage: The full per curiam opinion, the syllabus, and Justice Sotomayor's dissent (joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson) were read from the Supreme Court's preliminary print at https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/607us2r21_2bo2.pdf, which the Court's October Term 2025 slip opinion page lists for Zorn v. Linton. The preliminary print carries the official citation 607 U.S. 568 (2026), docket No. 25-297, decided March 23, 2026. The preliminary print is subject to formal revision before the bound volume is published.
Pin cites in this brief are to the preliminary print pagination (pages 568 to 582).

The Second Circuit opinion (135 F.4th 19 (2d Cir. 2025)) and Amnesty America v. West Hartford (361 F.3d 113 (2d Cir. 2004)) were not read. They are described only as the Supreme Court majority and dissent described them. The majority and dissent disagree about what the record shows regarding the timing of the first warning; both versions are stated in the brief.
The case was decided on the petition for certiorari without oral argument. The majority opinion is per curiam.

On April 20, 2026, the Court granted certiorari, vacated, and remanded Smith v. Scott (No. 24-1099) to the Ninth Circuit for further consideration in light of Zorn v. Linton. That order was read from the Court's April 20, 2026 order list and is described in the companion brief on Scott v. Smith.
facts:
The facts are as the Supreme Court stated them, viewed in the light most favorable to Linton because the case arose on the sergeant's motion for summary judgment. On January 8, 2015, Vermont held the Governor's inauguration at the state capitol. About 200 protesters attended, and some staged a sit in to demand universal healthcare. Shela Linton joined them. She planned to refuse to leave and anticipated being forcibly removed; she later said that was the point of the sit in.

When the capitol closed for the night, 29 protesters remained in the legislative chamber, sitting on the floor with arms linked. Officers explained that they would arrest the protesters for trespass if they did not leave. The officers dealt with them one at a time. Some stood and were escorted out without force; others refused to stand and were lifted to their feet or dragged out. A trooper described the safety threat as very low, and none of the demonstrators used violence.

After removing more than a dozen protesters, officers turned to Linton. Sergeant Jacob Zorn crouched to speak with her, but she remained seated with her arms interlocked with other protesters. As Linton passively resisted, Zorn unlinked her arm, put it behind her back in a rear wristlock, and twisted her arm. Linton exclaimed in pain while Zorn repeatedly asked her to please stand up. She said she would not. Zorn told her he would ask one more time and then would use more pain compliance. Linton again refused, so Zorn placed pressure on her wrist and lifted her by her underarm. Linton yelled as she stood. Once on her feet she continued to jerk her arms and fell back to the floor. Zorn asked her to stand again; when she did not, three officers picked her up by her arms and legs and carried her outside without further pain compliance. Linton alleged permanent damage to her left wrist and shoulder and post traumatic stress disorder, depression, and anxiety.

The dissent emphasized record facts favorable to Linton: that when officers first approached, they issued no clear request or command, saying only "ma'am?", that Zorn applied the wristlock about five seconds later without warning, and that his requests to stand and his warning about more pain compliance came only after the wristlock was already on.

Linton sued Zorn under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 for excessive force under the Fourth Amendment. The district court granted summary judgment to Zorn on qualified immunity, reasoning that it was not clearly established that lifting Linton while applying wrist pressure violated the Fourth Amendment in these circumstances. The Second Circuit reversed, holding that Amnesty America v. West Hartford clearly established that the gratuitous use of a rear wristlock on a passively resisting protester is excessive force, and remanded for trial. Judge Cabranes dissented, calling it a routine arrest and removal. Zorn petitioned for certiorari.
holding:
Certiorari granted and the judgment of the Second Circuit reversed, per curiam. The Court held that because the Second Circuit failed to identify a case where an officer using a routine wristlock on a protester after issuing a verbal warning, without more, was held to have violated the Constitution, Zorn was entitled to qualified immunity.

The standard. Officials have qualified immunity unless their conduct violates clearly established law, meaning law sufficiently clear that every reasonable official would have understood that what he is doing violates the right. Existing precedent must place the question beyond debate. Courts generally need to identify a case where an officer acting under similar circumstances was held to have violated the Constitution (Escondido v. Emmons). The precedent must define the right with a high degree of specificity (Wesby). General principles, such as that an officer may not use unreasonable and excessive force, do not suffice (Kisela). Officers receive immunity unless they could have read the relevant precedent beforehand and known it proscribed their specific conduct (Sheehan).

Amnesty America did not clearly establish the violation. Whether force is excessive depends on the facts of each case, including whether the officer gave warnings before using force, a point the Court supported by citing Barnes v. Felix. Amnesty America involved a wide range of allegations: officers rammed a protester's head into a wall, dragged another across the ground, and used rear wristlocks on two more to lift them before throwing one to the ground, with nothing indicating that any warning was given. Amnesty America did not hold that any of those actions violated the Fourth Amendment; it remanded for trial because a jury could find gratuitous pain but could also find the force reasonable. And it relied on a decision approving the practice of warning protesters and then using wristlocks to move them, the Ninth Circuit's Forrester v. City of San Diego. Reasonable officials would not read Amnesty America to establish that using a routine wristlock to move a resistant protester after warning her, without more, violates the Constitution. Zorn repeatedly warned Linton that he would have to use more force if she did not stand, and when she did not, he used a wristlock to bring her to her feet. Amnesty America never held that such conduct alone violated the Fourth Amendment; if anything it implied the opposite.

The general principle was too general. The Second Circuit read Amnesty America to establish that the gratuitous use of pain compliance techniques such as a rear wristlock on a passively resisting protester is excessive force. Even assuming Amnesty America established that principle, it lacks the high degree of specificity needed to make clear which actions violate the law, because it does not specify which circumstances make force gratuitous and does not obviously resolve whether a rear wristlock used to move a noncompliant protester after repeated warnings violates the Fourth Amendment.

Assumptions. In a footnote the Court assumed without deciding that controlling circuit precedent can clearly establish law for qualified immunity purposes.

The dissent. Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson, would have denied review. Taking the facts in Linton's favor, she concluded a jury could find excessive force: trespass is not a severe crime, the safety threat was very low, Linton suffered permanent loss of motion, there was a dispute whether she was actively or only passively resisting, officers did not use pain compliance on other protesters, and Zorn's own expert said the general practice against passive resistance is low level contact with little or no pain. On the clearly established prong she argued that Amnesty America specifically addressed rear wristlocks used to lift passively resisting protesters in a way that caused lasting damage and held those allegations sufficient to permit a finding of excessive force; that Amnesty America did involve warnings, because the officers there used the techniques only after failing to persuade the protesters verbally; and that on Linton's version Zorn gave no warning before applying the wristlock. She said the majority was effectively requiring a factually identical case, which the Court has repeatedly rejected, and that summary reversal was unwarranted because the Second Circuit applied a correctly stated standard to a particular set of facts. She repeated her view that the Court intervenes to reverse denials of qualified immunity far more readily than wrongful grants of it.
notDecided:
Whether Zorn's use of force actually violated the Fourth Amendment. The Court decided only that the law was not clearly established and did not address the first prong of qualified immunity. The dissent would have found a triable issue on the merits.

Whether controlling circuit precedent can clearly establish law for qualified immunity purposes. The Court assumed so without deciding.

Whether Amnesty America actually established the general principle the Second Circuit drew from it. The Court assumed it did and held the principle too general.

Whether a rear wristlock used without any warning on a passively resisting protester would violate clearly established law. The holding is framed around a routine wristlock used after a verbal warning, without more. The dissent's reading of the record, that the first warning came after the wristlock was applied, was not adopted by the majority.

Anything about pain compliance as a matter of policy or best practice. The Court cited Forrester as a decision approving warning protesters and then using wristlocks, but it did not itself endorse any technique.
inPractice:
Zorn is the Supreme Court's most recent word on how specific the law must be before an officer loses qualified immunity, and it arose from the kind of control hold taught in every arrest and control course.

The practical holding has three parts. First, the plaintiff must point to a case where an officer in similar circumstances was held to have violated the Constitution. Second, a general principle, even one stated by a circuit court, is not enough if it does not say which circumstances make force unlawful; the phrase gratuitous pain compliance did not tell officers what was forbidden. Third, warnings matter. The Court distinguished Amnesty America in part because nothing there indicated the officers warned the protesters, and it cited Barnes v. Felix for the proposition that warnings are part of the reasonableness picture. It also pointed to Forrester, which approved warning protesters and then using wristlocks to move them.

Officers should not read Zorn as approval of any particular technique or as a ruling that the force was reasonable. The Court did not decide that question. Three Justices concluded a jury could find the force excessive, and the dissent's version of the record, in which the wristlock went on before any warning, is a reminder that the sequence will be scrutinized.

Dr. Sowards teaches Zorn with Anderson v. Creighton, Malley v. Briggs, and Saucier v. Katz as the qualified immunity line: the reasonably well trained officer, clearly established law, and specificity. The training lesson is that a warning, a request for compliance, and a measured escalation are both what reasonable officers do and what courts look for. Qualified immunity protects officers whose conduct the law has not clearly condemned; it is not a reason to skip the steps that make force reasonable in the first place.
trainIt:
Teach the sequence Zorn used and the sequence the dissent described, side by side. Majority: crouch and speak, unlink the arm, apply the wristlock, request compliance repeatedly, warn that more pain compliance is coming, then apply pressure and lift. Dissent: a single word, five seconds, wristlock applied with no command, then requests and a warning. Have students build the version they would want on video: a clear command, a specific warning of what will happen, an opportunity to comply, then the lowest level of force that accomplishes the task. Zorn held that the law was not clearly established; it did not say the dissent's version was good practice.

Teach passive resistance as a distinct category. The Court's holding is limited to a routine wristlock on a resistant protester after a warning, without more. Pair Zorn with Forrester, which the Court cited as approving the practice of warning protesters and then using wristlocks to move them, and with Headwaters Forest Defense and other cases in the less lethal line that limit what may be done to passively resisting people. Students should be able to explain why a pain compliance hold on a seated, nonviolent person is low level force and why it still must be justified.

Teach the mechanics of the rear wristlock with attention to injury. Linton alleged permanent wrist and shoulder damage. Instructors should teach the hold with control of the angle and the lift, release of pressure on compliance, and the transition to a carry when the person will not stand, which is what the officers did after Linton fell.

Teach the qualified immunity rule accurately. Students should be able to state that the plaintiff must identify a case with similar circumstances, that general principles do not suffice, and that the Court did not decide whether the force was reasonable.
caution: The opinion was read in full from the Supreme Court's preliminary print, which is subject to formal revision. Zorn is a per curiam summary reversal on the clearly established prong only. It did not decide whether the wristlock was reasonable, did not approve any technique, and was decided on the majority's reading of a disputed record; the dissent read the record to show that the wristlock was applied before any warning. The brief should be taught as a qualified immunity case, not as a ruling that pain compliance on passive resisters is constitutional.
dissent: Justice Sotomayor dissented, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson. She would have denied certiorari. On the merits she said a reasonable jury could find excessive force because trespass is not a severe crime, the safety threat was very low, Linton suffered permanent loss of motion in her wrist and shoulder, there was a factual dispute whether she was only passively resisting and in too much pain to comply, officers did not use pain compliance on the other protesters, and Zorn's own expert said general practice against passive resistance is low level contact with little or no pain. On the clearly established prong she said Amnesty America specifically identified rear wristlocks used to lift passively resisting protesters in a way that caused lasting damage as sufficient to permit a finding of excessive force, that Amnesty America did involve warnings because the officers there used pain compliance only after verbal efforts failed, and that on Linton's version Zorn applied the wristlock without any warning. She said the majority's distinctions amounted to requiring a factually identical case, that the Second Circuit had applied a correctly stated standard, and that the case did not warrant the extraordinary remedy of summary reversal. She closed by repeating her criticism of what she called the Court's one sided approach to qualified immunity.

applications.title: Find the similar case
applications.body: To defeat qualified immunity a plaintiff generally must identify a case where an officer acting under similar circumstances was held to have violated the Constitution. A circuit opinion that remanded for trial on a wide range of allegations did not do that for a warned, routine wristlock.

applications.title: General principles are not enough
applications.body: A rule against gratuitous pain compliance on passively resisting protesters lacked the high degree of specificity needed because it did not say which circumstances make force gratuitous. Officers are protected from liability under rules that general.

applications.title: Warnings matter
applications.body: The Court distinguished Amnesty America in part because nothing indicated the officers there gave any warning, and it cited Barnes v. Felix for the relevance of warnings. Tell the person what you need and what will happen if they refuse.

applications.title: Immunity is not a merits ruling
applications.body: The Court did not decide whether Zorn's force was reasonable. Three Justices thought a jury could find it excessive. Qualified immunity protects an officer from damages; it does not make the force a model.

applications.title: The record will be read frame by frame
applications.body: The majority and dissent disagreed about whether the warning came before or after the wristlock was applied. The sequence of command, warning, and force is what reviewers will reconstruct from video.

quiz.q: On which prong of qualified immunity did the Supreme Court decide Zorn v. Linton?
options: The first prong: the Court held the wristlock was reasonable
The second prong: the Court held the law was not clearly established and did not decide whether the force was reasonable
Neither; the Court remanded for trial
quiz.teach: The Court held that the Second Circuit failed to identify a case holding that a routine wristlock on a protester after a verbal warning, without more, violated the Constitution. It did not address whether the force was excessive.

quiz.q: Why did the Court conclude that Amnesty America did not clearly establish the law for Zorn's conduct?
options: Because it was an unpublished decision
Because it involved a wide range of aggressive conduct with no indication of warnings, did not hold that any of it violated the Fourth Amendment, and relied on a case approving warned wristlocks
Because it was decided after the arrest
Because it involved a different circuit
quiz.teach: The Court said reasonable officials would not read Amnesty America to establish that using a routine wristlock to move a resistant protester after warning her, without more, violates the Constitution; if anything it implied the opposite by citing Forrester.

quiz.q: What did the dissent say about the warnings in the two cases?
options: That warnings are irrelevant to reasonableness
That Amnesty America did involve warnings and that, on Linton's version, Zorn applied the wristlock before any warning
That Zorn gave more warnings than required
That the protesters in Amnesty America were violent
quiz.teach: The dissent read Amnesty America as involving pain compliance used only after verbal efforts failed, and read the record here as showing a wristlock applied without warning, with requests and a warning coming only afterward.
